stages.note: Your cluster gets a virtual node. Pods you send there run on the GPU in AWS. From here on, run the commands below, or ask your AI to run them one at a time.

steps.h: Point kubectl at your cluster
steps.d: Your cluster administrator gives you a kubeconfig file. The node list must show the nodes of the cluster that gets the GPU. The last command must print yes: the connector install needs cluster-admin rights.
steps.c:
export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces

steps.h: Check the version
steps.d: The Server Version must be 1.30 or later. The second command must print one line.
steps.c:
kubectl version
kubectl api-resources | grep validatingadmissionpolicies

steps.h: Write down two address ranges
steps.d: Find the address range for your cluster's pods and for its services. Write down both. You need them in the connector step. Your cluster administrator can tell you if you cannot find them.
steps.c:
kubectl get servicecidrs -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDRS:.spec.cidrs
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NODE:.metadata.name,PODCIDRS:.spec.podCIDRs
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.ClusterConfiguration}' | grep -E 'podSubnet|serviceSubnet'
steps.g: The first two commands work on any cluster with Kubernetes 1.33 or later. The last command works on kubeadm clusters and shows the whole pod range. k3s: the defaults are 10.42.0.0/16 (pods) and 10.43.0.0/16 (services), unless your k3s server uses --cluster-cidr or --service-cidr. The node podCIDRs are slices of the pod range: with several nodes, ask your cluster administrator for the whole range. Other clusters: ask your cluster administrator.

steps.h: Check that your cluster can reach its apps
steps.d: It must print ok (or OK). A 502 means this cluster cannot reach the addresses of its own apps (this happens with OrbStack Kubernetes). Use another cluster, for example kind or k3s.
steps.c:
P=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/pods/$P:8080/proxy/health"

steps.h: Find your cluster's network software
steps.d: The output names the network software in your cluster, for example calico, cilium or flannel. Tell your Multicloud contact.
steps.c: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o name | grep -E 'cilium|calico|flannel|weave|antrea|canal'

steps.h: Check that your cluster has spare room
steps.d: The Multicloud node needs about 115m of spare CPU on one of your machines. If every machine is 95% or more used, add a machine first.
steps.c: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A8 'Allocated resources'

steps.h: Check that your cluster can reach the internet
steps.d: Good result: docker hub 401, ghcr 401, cloudflare 200. A connection or certificate error means your network blocks the connector. Nothing needs to reach your cluster from outside. If you use a company web proxy or TLS inspection, tell your Multicloud contact.
in: Egress path: direct, proxy or TLS inspection

steps.h: Check that your cluster can send UDP 51820 out
steps.d: The bridge in your cluster connects out to the Multicloud machines over WireGuard on UDP port 51820. Your network must allow outbound UDP 51820 from every cluster node (or from your NAT gateway) to any IPv4 address, from any source port, with return traffic allowed (a stateful firewall does this). The machine addresses change, so a fixed address list does not work. Nothing needs to reach your cluster from outside. A firewall change can take days: ask your network team now, so it runs while you wait for quota. To test: on a computer outside your network with a public address, allow inbound UDP 51820 and run nc -u -l 51820 (some nc versions need nc -u -l -p 51820). Then run the command with that address. The text multicloud-udp-test appears on that computer: the port is open. Nothing appears: the port is blocked. The command exits 0 in both cases, so only the outside computer shows the result. No outside computer: get a written yes from your network team. The bridge stage proves the path at the end.
in: Outbound UDP 51820: test passed, confirmed by the network team, or firewall request open
steps.c:
kubectl run udp-check --rm -i --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- sh -c \
  'echo multicloud-udp-test | nc -u -w 2 <outside-ip> 51820'

stages.note: A pool is the capacity in your AWS account that Multicloud manages for you. The pool keeps one worker running while it is awake, and you pay AWS for that worker. Create the pool only when your GPU quota is 4 or more.

steps.h: Create your GPU machines
steps.d: Replace <cloud-account-id> with your cloud account ID. These machines are GPU machines (L4 or A10G) that you pay for by the hour, never interrupted, with a 100 GB disk for the model. The cap is $1.50 per hour.
steps.c:
cat > poc-gpu.json <<'EOF'
{"settings": {"regions": ["us-east-1"], "accelerator_names": ["L4", "A10G"],
              "max_risk": 0, "min_storage_gb": 100,
              "max_memory_gb": 16}}
EOF
mctl extend create poc-gpu --cloud-account <cloud-account-id> --max-servers 2 \
  --max-cost-per-hour 1.5 --from-file poc-gpu.json

steps.h: Wait until the machines are ready
steps.d: Open https://multicloud.io/console/pools in your browser to follow the creation. Then return to this chat. The agent keeps checking here until the status says ready. The first start takes several minutes. If it is still starting after 20 minutes, send the output to your Multicloud contact.
steps.c:
cmd.exe /c start "" "https://multicloud.io/console/pools"   # opens the pools page in the Windows browser
mctl pool show poc-gpu

steps.h: Pause the machines when you stop for the day
steps.d: Paused machines cost nothing. Start them again when you continue.
steps.c:
mctl pool hibernate poc-gpu
mctl pool wake poc-gpu --wait

stages.note: A CPU pool for burst work. The pool keeps one worker running while it is awake, and you pay AWS for that worker.

steps.h: Create your CPU machines
steps.d: Replace <cloud-account-id> and the region. Up to three machines, at most $0.50 per hour together. If a pool with this name already exists and is hibernated, wake it instead of creating one: mctl pool wake <pool> --wait.
steps.c:
cat > burst.json <<'EOF'
{"settings": {"regions": ["us-east-1"]}}
EOF
mctl extend create burst --cloud-account <cloud-account-id> --max-servers 3 \
  --max-cost-per-hour 0.5 --from-file burst.json

steps.h: Wait until the machines are ready
steps.d: Open https://multicloud.io/console/pools in your browser to follow the creation. Then return to this chat. The agent keeps checking here until the status says ready. If it is still starting after 20 minutes, send the output to your Multicloud contact.
steps.c:
cmd.exe /c start "" "https://multicloud.io/console/pools"   # opens the pools page in the Windows browser
mctl pool show burst

stages.t: Connect your cluster to the pool
stages.note: Your Multicloud contact joins you for this stage. Check first that kubectl points at your own cluster (kubectl config current-context).

steps.h: Check that your cluster has no Multicloud software yet
steps.d: The cluster runs one liqo-consumer release. A new pool's peering needs that release replaced, and helm upgrade cannot do it: Liqo refuses a changed cluster ID. Show the release and its consumer ID, and the pool whose virtual node it serves. Tell the user that replacing it removes that pool's virtual node and link. After a yes: helm uninstall liqo-consumer -n liqo --wait. If a Liqo pre-delete hook fails because the controller is gone, helm uninstall liqo-consumer -n liqo --no-hooks, then remove leftover hook jobs. Then install the new release with the new peering's install command.
steps.c:
if helm list -n liqo -o json | jq -e 'length > 0' >/dev/null; then
  echo 'liqo-consumer is installed: stop'
  helm get values liqo-consumer -n liqo | grep -E 'clusterID|remoteClusterID'
else
  echo 'no connector: continue'
fi

steps.h: Create the link (GPU)
steps.d: This link lets your cluster use one GPU from the GPU machines. Without --gpu 1, the link gets no GPU. Write down the link number the output shows (it starts with Peering). Copy the whole line after Install command: you need it in the next step.
steps.c:
mctl peering create poc-gpu --gpu 1 --cpu-millicores 4000 --memory-mb 14336 \
  --pods 110 --ephemeral-storage-mb 51200

steps.h: Create the link
steps.d: The output starts with Peering and a number: write it down. It also shows an Install command line. Copy that line for the next step.
steps.c: mctl peering create burst

steps.h: Install the Multicloud software in your cluster
steps.who: You run it, with your CIDRs
steps.d: Paste the command from the Install command line. Replace <POD_CIDR> and <SERVICE_CIDR> with the two address ranges you wrote down in the cluster check. Change nothing else. Use the chart version the Install command prints (0.4.0 when this was tested); 0.3.1 is the minimum. This is needed for every Multicloud customer, with or without the bridge: apps that already run keep no address until they restart.
steps.c:
helm install liqo-consumer oci://registry-1.docker.io/multicloud/liqo-consumer-chart \
  --version 0.3.1 -n liqo --create-namespace \
  --set liqo.ipam.podCIDR=<POD_CIDR> --set liqo.ipam.serviceCIDR=<SERVICE_CIDR> \
  --set liqo.discovery.config.clusterID=c-…  --set-string reflectionKick.remoteClusterID=…

steps.h: Save the connection file
steps.d: Multicloud gives the connection file only once, on the first read after the peering is ready. This loop waits for it and saves it. Replace <peering-id> and <pool>: poc-gpu for the GPU route, burst for the CPU route. The file must not be empty. Keep it secret: it grants access to the pool. Do not run mctl peering show by hand before the loop ends.
steps.c:
POOL=<pool> ID=<peering-id>
(
  umask 077
  while true; do
    if mctl peering show "$POOL" "$ID" --json > peering.new; then
      mv peering.new peering.json
      jq -e '.bundle != null' peering.json >/dev/null && break
      st=$(jq -r .status peering.json); echo "Status: $st"
      [ "$st" = PENDING ] || break
    else
      rc=$?; [ "$rc" -eq 3 ] || [ "$rc" -eq 4 ] && { echo "mctl exit $rc: stop"; break; }
    fi
    sleep 10
  done
  rm -f peering.new
  jq -er '.bundle // empty' peering.json > multicloud-peering.yaml && rm peering.json
)
steps.g: If the status is SUSPENDED, wake the pool (mctl pool wake poc-gpu --wait) and run the loop again. If the status is FAILED or the file is empty, revoke the peering (mctl peering revoke poc-gpu <peering-id> --yes) and ask for one GPU again.

steps.h: Load the connection file into your cluster
steps.d: The check job name ends with your cluster's ID (c- and 8 characters), not the link number. Find that ID in the Install command line, in the clusterID part.
steps.c:
kubectl apply -f multicloud-peering.yaml
kubectl -n liqo wait --for=condition=complete --timeout=10m \
  job/multicloud-peering-preflight-<pool-slug>-<consumer-cluster-id>

steps.h: Check that the GPU shows up in your cluster
steps.d: The Multicloud node needs about 2 minutes. The output must be 1. An empty output in the first minutes is normal: run it again.
steps.c:
kubectl get node -l liqo.io/type=virtual-node \
  -o jsonpath='{..allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}'

steps.h: Update an older install
steps.who: You run it, with your CIDRs
steps.d: Only if Multicloud software below version 0.3.1 is already installed. Keep the same values, then restart the apps that already run (the restart step below).
steps.c:
helm upgrade liqo-consumer oci://registry-1.docker.io/multicloud/liqo-consumer-chart \
  --version 0.3.1 -n liqo --reset-then-reuse-values \
  --set liqo.ipam.podCIDR=<POD_CIDR> --set liqo.ipam.serviceCIDR=<SERVICE_CIDR>

steps.h: Check the Multicloud node
steps.d: The Multicloud node must say Ready and show the machine name in the last column. It needs about 2 minutes after the connection file is loaded.
steps.c: kubectl get nodes -l liqo.io/type=virtual-node -L multicloud.io/pool

stages.note: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fits the 24 GB of an L4 or A10G.

steps.h: Send this namespace to the Multicloud machines
steps.d: Only apps in a namespace sent to Multicloud can use its machines. Other apps in my-apps still run on your own machines.
steps.c:
kubectl create namespace my-apps
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: offloading.liqo.io/v1beta1
kind: NamespaceOffloading
metadata: {name: offloading, namespace: my-apps}
spec:
  namespaceMappingStrategy: DefaultName
  podOffloadingStrategy: LocalAndRemote
  clusterSelector:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - {key: liqo.io/type, operator: In, values: [virtual-node]}
EOF

steps.h: Create the model API key
steps.d: vLLM refuses a request without this key. The key stays in your cluster.
steps.c:
kubectl -n my-apps create secret generic vllm-api-key \
  --from-literal=key="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"

steps.h: Save the vLLM manifest
steps.d: Copy this block into a file named vllm-gpu.yaml in your current folder. On the command line: run cat > vllm-gpu.yaml, paste the block, press Enter, then Ctrl+D.

steps.h: Deploy vLLM and wait
steps.d: The first start takes up to about 20 minutes: a new GPU worker, the image and a 15 GB model download. The wait command returns when the model is loaded.
steps.c:
kubectl -n my-apps apply -f vllm-gpu.yaml
kubectl -n my-apps wait --for=condition=available deploy/vllm --timeout=30m
steps.g: To watch the progress, run kubectl -n my-apps get pod -l app=vllm -o wide -w in another terminal. Press Ctrl+C to stop the watch.

steps.h: Open the local port
steps.d: Open a new terminal (on Windows: a new Ubuntu window), point it at your cluster again (export KUBECONFIG=…), and run the command. Keep this terminal open while you send queries. Send the queries from your first terminal.
steps.c: kubectl -n my-apps port-forward deploy/vllm 8000:8000
steps.c_agent:
mkdir -p ~/multicloud-onboarding && chmod 700 ~/multicloud-onboarding
nohup kubectl -n my-apps port-forward deploy/vllm 8000:8000 >~/multicloud-onboarding/port-forward.log 2>&1 &
echo $! > ~/multicloud-onboarding/port-forward.pid

steps.h: Send your first query
steps.d: See “Send a query to the model” below.
steps.c_agent:
KEY=$(kubectl -n my-apps get secret vllm-api-key -o jsonpath='{.data.key}' | base64 -d)
curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"qwen","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello."}]}' | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'
unset KEY

stages.note: A small pod on the pool proves the path.

steps.h: Send this namespace to the Multicloud machines
steps.d: Only apps in a namespace sent to Multicloud can use its machines.
steps.c:
kubectl create namespace my-apps
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: offloading.liqo.io/v1beta1
kind: NamespaceOffloading
metadata: {name: offloading, namespace: my-apps}
spec:
  namespaceMappingStrategy: DefaultName
  podOffloadingStrategy: LocalAndRemote
  clusterSelector:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - {key: liqo.io/type, operator: In, values: [virtual-node]}
EOF

steps.h: Run a test app on the Multicloud machines
steps.d: Replace <slug> with the machine name from the Multicloud node check. The NODE column must show the Multicloud node. A machine that was paused needs about 5 minutes to start.
steps.c:
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: burst-hello, namespace: my-apps}
spec:
  tolerations:
  - {key: multicloud.io/pool, operator: Equal, value: <slug>, effect: NoSchedule}
  nodeSelector: {multicloud.io/pool: <slug>}
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hello from the pool; uname -n; sleep 30"]
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}
EOF
kubectl -n my-apps wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/burst-hello --timeout=15m
kubectl -n my-apps get pod burst-hello -o wide
kubectl -n my-apps logs burst-hello
kubectl -n my-apps delete pod burst-hello

stages.t: Reach the pool from your cluster (Extend proxy)
stages.note: Required for every Extend use case. Without the proxy, a pod in your cluster cannot call a pod on the pool. The skill brings the proxy file. Multicloud turns on the pool network for your pool.

steps.h: Run a small web server on the pool
steps.d: The CPU test app is a pod that exits, so the bridge has nothing to reach. This runs nginx, a small public web server with no GPU, on the pool in my-apps, as Service nginx on port 80. Its page says 'hello from the pool', so the tunnel test has a known answer. It listens on IPv6 too, because the proxy reaches pods by their IPv6 address. It costs nothing beyond the pool node. Replace <slug> with the pool slug from the node check. Cleanup removes it with the namespace my-apps.
steps.c:
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: nginx, namespace: my-apps}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: nginx}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: nginx}}
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - {key: multicloud.io/pool, operator: Equal, value: <slug>, effect: NoSchedule}
      nodeSelector: {multicloud.io/pool: <slug>}
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27-alpine
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hello from the pool > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html && sed -i 's/listen  *80;/listen 80; listen [::]:80;/' /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf && exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]
        ports: [{containerPort: 80, name: http}]
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: 10m, memory: 32Mi}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: nginx, namespace: my-apps}
spec:
  selector: {app: nginx}
  ports: [{name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http}]
EOF
kubectl -n my-apps wait --for=condition=Available deploy/nginx --timeout=15m

steps.h: Set up the bridge
steps.who: You, with the agent (it fills the file and shows you the result)
steps.d: The bridge file comes with this skill (assets/extend-proxy.yaml), so you need nothing from anyone else. The agent copies it to your home folder, fills in your pool name, your link number and the route (my-apps, service vllm, port 8000), checks that nothing is left to fill in, and shows you the result. It loads the file only on your yes. This step comes after your first app runs, because the route needs the namespace my-apps to exist and be offloaded. The namespace multicloud-extend-proxy is never labelled for Liqo offloading. A second bridge in the same cluster needs its own copy of the file with its own namespace.

in.label: Link number (from the link step, starts with Peering)

steps.c:
F="$HOME/multicloud-onboarding/extend-proxy.yaml"
mkdir -p "$HOME/multicloud-onboarding" && cp "<skill-folder>/assets/extend-proxy.yaml" "$F" && chmod 600 "$F"
POOL="<pool>"; PEER="<peering-id>"; SVC="vllm"; PORT="8000"
sed -i.bak -e "s|<pool>|$POOL|" -e "s|<peering-id>|$PEER|" -e "s|<service>|$SVC|" -e "s|<service-port>|$PORT|" "$F" && rm -f "$F.bak"
! grep -v '^ *#' "$F" | grep -n '<'   # prints nothing when every placeholder is filled
# client dry-run: a server dry-run needs the namespace, which only the apply creates
kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f "$F"
# after your yes:
kubectl apply -f "$F"
steps.g: An install from an older copy of the file used the names extend-proxy-discovery. Only if they exist: kubectl -n my-apps get role,rolebinding extend-proxy-discovery. If they do, delete them after your yes (deletes cannot be undone).

steps.h: Set up the bridge
steps.who: You, with the agent (it fills the file and shows you the result)
steps.d: The bridge file comes with this skill (assets/extend-proxy.yaml), so you need nothing from anyone else. The agent copies it to your home folder, fills in your pool name, your link number and the route (my-apps, service nginx, port 80), checks that nothing is left to fill in, and shows you the result. It loads the file only on your yes. This step comes after your first app runs, because the route needs the namespace my-apps to exist and be offloaded. The namespace multicloud-extend-proxy is never labelled for Liqo offloading. A second bridge in the same cluster needs its own copy of the file with its own namespace.

in.label: Link number (from the link step, starts with Peering)

steps.c:
F="$HOME/multicloud-onboarding/extend-proxy.yaml"
mkdir -p "$HOME/multicloud-onboarding" && cp "<skill-folder>/assets/extend-proxy.yaml" "$F" && chmod 600 "$F"
POOL="<pool>"; PEER="<peering-id>"; SVC="nginx"; PORT="80"
sed -i.bak -e "s|<pool>|$POOL|" -e "s|<peering-id>|$PEER|" -e "s|<service>|$SVC|" -e "s|<service-port>|$PORT|" "$F" && rm -f "$F.bak"
! grep -v '^ *#' "$F" | grep -n '<'   # prints nothing when every placeholder is filled
# client dry-run: a server dry-run needs the namespace, which only the apply creates
kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f "$F"
# after your yes:
kubectl apply -f "$F"
steps.g: An install from an older copy of the file used the names extend-proxy-discovery. Only if they exist: kubectl -n my-apps get role,rolebinding extend-proxy-discovery. If they do, delete them after your yes (deletes cannot be undone).

steps.h: Create the bridge key in your cluster
steps.who: You approve; the agent runs it. Multicloud makes the key and saves it in your cluster. Nobody sees it.
steps.d: The bridge key lets the bridge sign in to Multicloud. Multicloud makes it for you and saves it in your cluster, in the namespace multicloud-extend-proxy, so you never copy it. The key can only run this bridge. It is not shown on screen, not printed and not written to a file. You need to be an owner of your Multicloud organization. It runs after the bridge file is applied, because the key is saved in the namespace that file creates. Run it with --replace only when you want a new key: the old key then keeps working until you revoke it in the console.
steps.c: mctl extend proxy-key create --pool <pool> --kube-context <context>
steps.g: Not signed in: run mctl auth login first. Several organizations: add --org <org>. Needs mctl 0.12.0 or later (mctl --version). <context> is the context from the cluster check (kubectl config current-context).

steps.h: Check that the bridge is ready
steps.d: Needs the machines awake, the link ready, the namespace my-apps sent to Multicloud, and Multicloud software version 0.3.1 or later (helm list -n liqo). Both bridge copies must show READY 1/1. If the machines are paused, the bridge shows not ready: do not act, it becomes ready when the machines start. If the log says HOST_FIREWALL_OFF, ask Multicloud to turn on the machine network; the bridge retries by itself. The first registration can take a few minutes; the log shows registration retries, then a registered line. Before that, check the pool: mctl pool show <pool> --json must show managed.host_firewall true. If it is false, the log shows HOST_FIREWALL_OFF: ask Multicloud to turn the host firewall on for the pool. Both copies stay 0/1 after a registered line, with no HOST_FIREWALL_OFF: outbound UDP 51820 is most likely blocked (step udp-51820 in the cluster stage). The log does not name this cause. Ask your network team to open the port, and ask Multicloud to check the pool side: 0 fresh handshakes means no packet from the bridge arrives.
steps.c:
kubectl -n multicloud-extend-proxy get pods
kubectl -n multicloud-extend-proxy logs deploy/extend-proxy --tail=20

steps.h: Restart apps that already run
steps.d: An offloaded pod that has not restarted since the chart change has no address. The proxy skips it. Restart each deployment (or statefulset) in my-apps. After the restart, the IP column shows an fd00:244:... address. On a first run there are no such pods: skip this step. A pod that no controller owns needs kubectl delete pod and a new kubectl apply. Node-level DaemonSets do not run on the virtual node, so they need no restart.
steps.c:
kubectl -n my-apps rollout restart deployment/<name>
kubectl -n my-apps get pods -o wide

steps.h: Test the bridge from an app in your cluster
steps.d: Run it only after the first workload runs on the pool (deploy-vllm in run-gpu-llm, or proxy-target for the CPU use case). Before that, leave it and come back. The test pod runs in a namespace that is not offloaded, so it stays on your own nodes. Any HTTP status code means the path works: for vLLM a 401 is normal (it needs its API key); the CPU service answers 200. A timeout or a DNS error means it does not: check proxy-check and HOST_FIREWALL_OFF.
steps.c:
kubectl -n default run proxy-test --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.10.1 -- \
  curl -sS -m 10 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://vllm-pool.multicloud-extend-proxy.svc:8000/

steps.h: Test through the tunnel from your computer
steps.d: A tunnel carries the request from your computer, through your cluster and the proxy, to the pool. Keep the first window open while you test. Run the second command in a second window. CPU use case: the answer is 'hello from the pool'. GPU use case (vLLM): a 401 is the right answer without the key; ask for a model answer with the key from the vLLM step to see the model reply.
steps.c:
# window 1: the tunnel (keep it open)
kubectl -n multicloud-extend-proxy port-forward svc/vllm-pool 8000:8000
# window 2: the test
curl -sS -m 10 http://localhost:8000/

stages.note: A GPU worker costs about $0.80–$1.20 per hour while it runs. To pause instead of delete, use mctl pool hibernate poc-gpu. Delete in this order.

steps.h: Remove the PoC from your cluster and Multicloud
steps.d: Stop the port-forward first (Ctrl+C). The proxy goes first: when it stops, it removes its registration with its key. Then revoke the extend-proxy key in Account › API keys. Replace <peering-id>. Delete the bundle before the revoke: a revoke first makes the bundle delete hang on Liqo finalizers. After the bundle delete, Liqo cannot clear its own finalizers, so the for loop clears them. Do not delete the liqo namespace before helm uninstall finishes. Deleting the pool cannot be undone.
steps.c:
kubectl delete namespace multicloud-extend-proxy --ignore-not-found
kubectl -n my-apps delete -f vllm-gpu.yaml
kubectl -n my-apps delete secret vllm-api-key
kubectl delete namespaceoffloadings.offloading.liqo.io --all -A
kubectl delete -f multicloud-peering.yaml --wait=false
for t in namespacemaps.offloading.liqo.io resourceslices.authentication.liqo.io; do
  kubectl get $t -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{" "}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' |
    while read ns n; do kubectl -n "$ns" patch $t "$n" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'; done
done
mctl peering revoke poc-gpu <peering-id> --yes
kubectl delete foreignclusters.core.liqo.io --all
helm uninstall liqo-consumer -n liqo --wait --timeout 10m
kubectl delete namespace liqo my-apps
mctl pool delete poc-gpu --yes

steps.h: Check that nothing is left
steps.d: Wait a few minutes after the pool delete. Both commands must print nothing. If a Multicloud instance still shows after 15 minutes, tell your Multicloud contact. Replace <region> with the pool region (repeat the command for each region of the pool), and run it with an AWS sign-in to the account (export AWS_PROFILE=<profile>). A new account that Multicloud's Terraform made: skip the aws command if you have no sign-in there; closing the account in the next step removes everything in it.
steps.c:
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations | grep liqo
aws ec2 describe-instances --region <region> \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running Name=tag-key,Values=multicloud-cluster-id \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType]' --output text

steps.h: Path A: close the new AWS account
steps.d: Only for a new account that Multicloud's Terraform created, and only when you do not keep it after the PoC. Run it in the folder you made when you connected AWS (the folder with multicloud.tf), with the same AWS profile (the management account). It disconnects the account, waits until Multicloud has cleaned up, removes the role and closes the AWS account. AWS keeps a closed account for 90 days, and its email cannot be used for a new AWS account again. mctl asks you to confirm: type y. Path B of “Set up your AWS account” (an IAM user with an access key): after the PoC, deactivate and delete the key (IAM › Users › poc-admin › Security credentials › Actions › Deactivate, then Delete).
steps.c:
cd <connection-folder>
export AWS_PROFILE=<profile> AWS_REGION=<region>
mctl cloud-account destroy <cloud-account-id>

steps.h: Path B: remove Multicloud from an account you have
steps.d: Only for an account you have, and only when you do not keep the connection after the PoC. Run the commands one at a time, in the folder you made when you connected AWS, with the same AWS profile. The disconnect stops Multicloud and removes what it created in your account. If tofu state list prints only data.* and random_id lines, there is nothing to destroy: stop there. Otherwise tofu destroy removes the role; type yes. The destroy does not use the connect token, so any value works for it. Path B of “Set up your AWS account” (an IAM user with an access key): after the PoC, deactivate and delete the key (IAM › Users › poc-admin › Security credentials › Actions › Deactivate, then Delete).
in: Approve: disconnect and remove the role
steps.c:
cd <connection-folder>
export AWS_PROFILE=<profile> AWS_REGION=<region>
mctl cloud-account disconnect <cloud-account-id> --wait
tofu state list
TF_VAR_multicloud_connect_token=unused tofu destroy
